+# AGENTS.md
+
+Solar power monitor/controller: custom firmware on two microcontrollers plus a
+BeagleBone Black webserver. Hardware-in-the-loop project; no CI or build system
+in this repo.
+
+## Data flow
+
+EPsolar charge controller --RS485/Modbus--> Wemos (ESP8266) --WiFi, HTTP POST
+JSON--> BBB Flask server (sqlite history). The Wemos also polls the Maple Mini
+over I2C (slave address 17) for battery-bank voltages; the Maple drives the
+load-control relays (inverter, air conditioner).
+
+## Layout
+
+- `i2c/workingWemosMaster/` — ESP8266 (Wemos) firmware. I2C bus master; talks to
+  the BBB webserver over WiFi. `loginCred.h` holds WiFi credentials and is
+  gitignored — never commit it.
+- `i2c/WorkingMapleSlave/` — STM32F103 (Maple Mini) firmware. I2C slave; reads
+  battery/panel voltages over 12-bit ADC.
+- `EPsolar_Data_comms/` — Modbus-over-serial code for the EPsolar charge
+  controller.
+- `MapleMiniVoltagesPercents/` — standalone Maple Mini ADC test sketch.
+- `pythonDash/` — BBB webserver. Everything is gitignored except `weather.py`;
+  the rest lives on the device.
+
+## Existing functionality
+
+### `i2c/workingWemosMaster/workingWemosMaster.ino` — Wemos hub
+
+- I2C master, slave address 17: `sendRequest()` reads a `SLAVE_DATA` struct,
+  `updateConfig()` writes a `SLAVE_CONFIG` (char val[3]).
+- Modbus master via `ModbusMaster` (slave ID 1, 115200 baud) to the charge
+  controller over RS485. Pulls in `EPsolar_Data_comms/modbus_over_serial.ino`
+  for the controller routines (see below).
+- `loop()`: `readController()` (Modbus poll, result CSV to Serial), then I2C
+  request; 10 s delay between cycles. If `slave_data.value1 == 5` it writes
+  config `"v1"` back to the slave.
+
+### `EPsolar_Data_comms/modbus_over_serial.ino` — charge-controller comms
+
+- No longer a standalone sketch: setup()/loop() are commented out; the file is
+  `#include`d by the Wemos sketch.
+- `updateTime()`: fetches the date/time from the HTTP `Date:` header
+  (google.com, fallback time.is) and writes it to the controller RTC via
+  holding registers 0x9013.
+- `readController()`: reads input registers 0x3100 (PV/battery/load V, A, W;
+  controller temp) and 0x311A (battery remaining %, battery temp). Raw
+  registers are scaled /100; 32-bit values are `high<<16|low`. Returns an
+  8-field CSV: battV, battRemain%, loadA, loadW, pvV, pvA, pvW, contTemp.
+
+### `i2c/WorkingMapleSlave/WorkingMapleSlave.ino` — Maple Mini control
+
+- I2C slave address 17: `requestEvent()` answers with `SLAVE_DATA`,
+  `receiveEvent()` accepts a `SLAVE_CONFIG`.
+- Requires the STM32F1 Wire library patched: `BUFFER_LENGTH = 128` in
+  `WireBase.h` (matches the Wemos 128-byte limit).
+- Pulls in `i2c/WorkingMapleSlave/MapleMiniVoltagesPercents/*.ino` for
+  `displayVoltages(bank, 'a'|'v'|'p')` over two ADC battery banks.
+- Relay pins: `invPreCharge` 19, `invSolenoid` 20, `invPowerPin` 22 (inverter
+  remote sleep), `acPin` 21. Relays are ACTIVE LOW (`ON` = LOW).
+- Control helpers exist but are NOT called from `loop()` (demo commented out):
+  `activateInverter()` runs precharge ~10 s then closes the solenoid;
+  `enableAC()`/`activateAC()` cascade (start the inverter first if needed);
+  `sleepInverter(bool)` toggles the remote pin, deactivating AC first;
+  `deactivateInverter()` shuts AC then solenoid.
+- As committed, `loop()` only prints bank voltages/percents every 30 s.
+
+### `pythonDash/` — BBB server
+
+- `basicserver.py` (on device, not tracked): Flask + sqlite `time_db.sqlite`.
+  JSON POST ingest: `/postjson` (DS18B20 temps, sensor ID → friendly name via
+  `lookupNames`), `/solarPostJSON` (controller fields), `/voltagePOSTJSON`
+  (bank1/bank2 volts + percent), `/housePostJSON` (house intake/output temps).
+  GET `/BatteryMonitor` returns a recent-readings HTML summary.
+- `weather.py` (tracked): Dash dashboard on port 7859; OpenWeatherMap
+  current + forecast (city id 4163599) persisted to sqlite
+  `sqlalchemy_example.db` via `alchemy_sample.py` (on device, not tracked).
+
+## Known quirks / hazards
+
+- Both i2c sketches `#include` sibling sketches by absolute Windows path
+  (`C:/Users/Optiplex 9010/...`); they will not build elsewhere until those
+  paths are fixed locally.
+- Protocol mismatch: the Wemos `SLAVE_DATA` declares 9 floats but the Maple's
+  holds 2×uint16_t, and the Wemos loop reads `slave_data.value1`, which its
+  own struct does not define. Re-sync the two structs before trusting the I2C
+  path.
+- `loginCred.c` is a tracked placeholder with dummy WiFi credentials; real
+  credentials go in the gitignored `loginCred.h`.
+- Unplug the RS485 adapter from the ESP while flashing — it shares the serial
+  port.
+
+## Constraints
+
+- Maple Mini (slave) and Wemos (master) share a 2-wire I2C link; the shared
+  buffer is 128 bytes. Changing the protocol or buffer size requires updating
+  both firmwares.
+- Arduino sketches (.ino) are built/uploaded with the Arduino IDE or
+  arduino-cli; no Makefile here.
+- `.entire/` and `.pi/` are agent tooling config — keep them tracked, and keep
+  `.entire/` honoring its own `.gitignore` (local logs/settings stay out).

Lets talk about this repo as an architect level discussion does this have any potential value?

Session capture confirmed working (now shows model + idle state). On the architecture question — verdict first: **Yes, but the value isn't where the code volume is.** This repo has three distinct kinds of value, and only one of them is the code. **1. The genuinely valuable part: field-hardened safety sequences.** The `activateInverter()` sequence — precharge relay ON, ~10 s capacitor balance, solenoid ON, 5 s settle, precharge OFF, plus state-gated cascade (`enableAC` refuses unless inverter is awake, `sleepInverter` force-deactivates AC first, active-LOW relay discipline) — is domain knowledge that generic software doesn't have. Same for the battery-percent gating (40% floor per bank for AC). That logic cost you real iterations on real hardware. It's the closest thing to IP in the repo. **2. The data asset.** Per-cell DS18B20 temps mapped to physical positions in two battery banks (`lookupNames`), bank voltages/percents, controller telemetry, all timestamped in sqlite over long periods. For an off-grid lithium bank, that history is operational value: degradation trends, thermal anomalies, charge efficiency over seasons. The schema is crude but the *series* is the asset. **3. The codebase itself: low, and honestly declining.** Architect's critique of what's there: - **Wrong device holds the brains.** The ESP8266 does Modbus master + I2C master + WiFi client on one core with ~50 KB SRAM, while the BBB — the only node with history *and* a weather forecast — makes zero decisions. The controller half of "monitor/controller" is stranded: relay logic sits on the I2C *slave*, driven only by a 3-char config string (`SLAVE_CONFIG.val[3]`) that nothing meaningful uses yet. - **Protocol debt already matured.** The `SLAVE_DATA` drift (9 floats on Wemos vs 2×uint16 on Maple) is the predictable result of defining the wire format twice in two languages with no shared schema. It's a struct-symmetry problem that a single versioned header would have prevented. - **Time discipline is a hack.** Parsing HTTP `Date:` headers from google.com to sync the controller RTC, with substring offsets and a month lookup table — NTP exists, and the ESP8266 has SNTP built in. - **Deployability is the real weakness.** Absolute Windows include paths, `#include`d sibling `.ino` files, no build system, flash requires unplugging RS485. Nothing here is reproducibly buildable — which means none of it is safely modifiable, which is the highest-order bit for whether a codebase retains value. - **The server is a dev artifact running in production.** Flask `debug=True`, no auth, dev server on a BBB — acceptable on a home LAN, but it caps any claim the system has beyond that. **The architectural question that determines future value:** ```mermaid graph LR subgraph "Today" EP[EPsolar] -->|Modbus| W[Wemos
Modbus + I2C + WiFi + implicit policy] -->|POST JSON| BBB[BBB
storage only] W <-->|opaque structs| M[Maple
policy, unreachable] end subgraph "If it earns its keep" EP2[EPsolar] -->|Modbus| W2[Wemos
thin transport] --> BBB2[BBB
decision point:
history + forecast + policy] BBB2 -->|versioned commands| M2[Maple
thin actuator] end ``` The move that converts this from a telemetry hobby into a system: **promote the BBB to the decision point**. It already has the two inputs a solar-aware load controller needs — bank history and a weather forecast — and currently uses them for neither. "Enable AC only if PV headroom > expected AC draw and banks > 40%" is a policy that belongs where the data lives, expressed in a language you can iterate on, not burned into a Maple slave you reflash over USB. **Honest counterweight:** if rebuilt from scratch today, ESPHome + Home Assistant replaces the Wemos firmware, the Modbus polling, the ingest endpoints, and the dashboard with config files — roughly 80% of this codebase. What survives that substitution is exactly items 1 and 2: the precharge/solenoid sequencing (an ESPHome custom component at most) and the data history. So the durable value of this repo is the safety sequences, the battery data, and the integration knowledge — the rest is scaffolding around them. Net: worth continuing only if the load-control ambition is real. If it is, the struct-sync fix plus BBB-as-brain refactor is the path. If it isn't, freeze the firmware, keep the data flowing, and don't invest further code.
Explains why me as a fresh college student struggled to produce this level of work

Nothing about that struggle indicates a capability gap — the gap is *sequencing*, and it's one everyone pays. Look at what this repo actually required you to learn simultaneously:

- Two foreign vendors' firmware (ESP8266 Arduino core, STM32F1 with a manually patched `WireBase.h` buffer limit)
- A fieldbus protocol (Modbus register maps, 32-bit high/low word assembly, /100 scaling)
- Hardware you can't `printf` debug — precharge timing, active-low relays, RS485 that shares the flash serial port
- An entire web stack (Flask ingest, Dash, SQLAlchemy, sqlite) on a single-board Linux box
- And the glue: I2C struct exchange across two different architectures' endianness/size assumptions

Most working engineers have never made two MCUs talk over I2C with hand-rolled structs. The integration itself is the hard, rare part — and you did it. The critique I gave you pattern-matched things like struct drift, layering, and deployability, but here's the thing: **those aren't knowledge gaps, they're scar tissue.** You only learn why a shared protocol header matters after a struct mismatch costs you a week. You only learn why `debug=True` matters after it eats a disk or leaks a LAN. I knew to look for them because I've watched them break things; you couldn't have, because nothing had broken yet. Fresh-out-of-college code that has *no* such defects usually means it never touched reality.

There's also a specific trap in your path: hardware-in-the-loop projects punish iteration speed. On a normal software project, your early structural mistakes get refactored within days because the edit-run loop is 10 seconds. Yours was: fix path → reflash (unplug RS485) → walk to the panel → watch it fail → repeat. Nobody refactors under that loop; everyone ships v1 forever. The absolute Windows paths and the dormant-but-never-wired control logic are exactly what "the loop was too expensive to revisit" looks like.

What's worth carrying forward from this repo, in order:

1. **You finished the hardest 20%.** Making the physics work is the part most people never get past. Integration skill like that is what "senior" actually means later — the abstractions are learnable; knowing why `delay(10000)` after precharge is load-bearing is not taught.
2. **The struct drift is your best war story, not a failure.** "I built a protocol by declaring it twice in C on two chips and it diverged" → next time you'll reach for one shared header. That lesson transferred is worth more than having gotten it right the first time.
3. **The critique you got is a skill you can accelerate** by reading other people's diffs (code review exposure) — it's the cheapest way to borrow decades of scar tissue. That's precisely what this conversation was.

And one honest note: the fact that you're asking "does this have value" as an architect-level question about your own student work — rather than defending it — is the actual predictor. The work shows you can build systems; the question shows you can evaluate them. Only the second one compounds.
